title: Insert into a full B-tree page
description: A new order ID lands on a leaf page with no room left. Trace the insert through the split and the write-ahead log.

problemStatement.overview:
The orders table in Postgres has a B-tree index on `order_id`. Unlike an LSM tree, a B-tree keeps data in fixed-size pages (8 KB in Postgres, 16 KB in InnoDB) and updates them in place.

That makes reads fast and predictable: a few page hops from root to leaf. The hard part is an insert into a page that's already full. The page must split, the parent must learn about the new page, and all of it must survive a crash halfway through.

The outline follows one insert. Fill the blocks. Traps describe an LSM tree or skip the safety net.
problemStatement.yourTask: Order the steps of inserting a key into a full B-tree leaf, from the root down to pages reaching disk.
yourTaskSteps: Fill each empty block from Unused.
hints: Find the right leaf before worrying about space.
A split touches the leaf, a new page, and the parent.
Changed pages can stay in memory for a while, as long as the log is on disk.
problemStatement.moat:
Setter notes, not shown to learners.

Required chain: descend-to-leaf → leaf-full → split-leaf → update-parent → write-wal → flush-later.
Optional splice: split-root on update-parent → write-wal.
Five traps.

platformSpec.passMessage: Descend, split, update the parent, log it, flush later. That's a B-tree insert.

pieces.title: Descend from the root to the leaf
pieces.blurb: Start at the root page and follow the child pointer whose key range contains the new order ID, down to a leaf page.

pieces.title: The leaf page has no free space
pieces.blurb: Pages have a fixed size. This leaf can't fit another entry.

pieces.title: Split the leaf into two pages
pieces.blurb: Allocate a new page, move the upper half of the keys into it, and insert the new key into whichever half it belongs to.

pieces.title: Add a pointer to the new page in the parent
pieces.blurb: Insert a separator key and a pointer to the new page into the parent, so searches can find both halves.

pieces.title: Parent full too: split up to the root
pieces.blurb: If the parent has no room, it splits as well, possibly all the way up. A root split creates a new root and the tree grows one level taller.

pieces.title: Log every changed page to the WAL
pieces.blurb: Write-ahead log records describing the split and the insert are written, and reach disk before any of the changed pages do.

pieces.title: Dirty pages are written to disk later
pieces.blurb: The modified pages stay in the buffer pool. A checkpoint or background writer flushes them eventually; after a crash, the WAL redoes them.

pieces.title: Append to a new file and merge later
pieces.blurb: Write the key to a fresh sorted file and let background compaction fold it into the index.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: That's an LSM tree. A B-tree updates fixed-size pages in place.

pieces.title: Shift the following pages to make room
pieces.blurb: Move every page after the full leaf one slot along the file so the leaf can grow.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Pages don't need to be contiguous. The new page can be allocated anywhere; pointers link them.

pieces.title: Rebalance the whole tree
pieces.blurb: After the insert, redistribute keys across every page so all leaves are equally full.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Only pages on the path from the leaf to the root are touched. A full rebalance would be absurdly expensive.

pieces.title: Add a new level below the leaves
pieces.blurb: When pages fill up, the tree grows deeper by hanging new pages underneath the current leaves.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: B-trees grow at the top. Only a root split adds a level, which keeps every leaf at the same depth.

pieces.title: Write the pages straight to disk, no log
pieces.blurb: Flush the leaf, the new page and the parent immediately, so there's nothing to log.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: A crash between those writes leaves a page pointing nowhere. The WAL is what makes a split atomic.
